title: Embeddings & Reranking perf/cost deep-dive
summary: Deep technical discussion focused on embedding dimensionality, batching strategies, and reranking pipeline tradeoffs. Customer is trying to hit sub-30ms p95 for first-stage embed lookup and sub-200ms end-to-end for rerank on 100 QPS. Discussed options: GPU vs CPU for embedding generation, Faiss configs (HNSW vs IVF+PQ), Redwood's KV cache semantics for prefix reuse, quantization tradeoffs and how Dedicated/Private deployments affect latency and costs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a small benchmark, share config templates and rough cost model, schedule follow-up to validate p95 targets on customer's infra.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the embedding + reranking perf and cost tradeoffs for the Novus use case. I'm Maya from Redwood, with Luis and Priya. Alex: yep thanks, we really want to understand whether to go hosted or private for our 100 qps workload.
[00:22] Alex Morgan: quick context, our flow is two-stage: first stage approximate nearest neighbor retrieval over 20M docs, then a lightweight neural reranker for top 100. target is sub-30ms p95 for first stage and end-to-end < 200ms p95.
[00:40] Luis Ortega: ok, ballpark — 20M at 768 dims, what's your vector dim today?
[00:47] Dana Lee: currently 1024 dims using our internal embedder, but we're experimenting with 768 and 512 to save cost.
[00:54] Priya Patel: important trade: lower dims reduce index size and distance compute but may reduce recall; we'll need evals. for perf, 512-> about 50% memory savings vs 1024.
[01:10] Samir Patel: our infra is GCP private VPC, we want option to keep data in VPC. curious on Dedicated vs Private for latency.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with predictable latency; Private (on-prem/VPC) lets you host inside your network but depends on your hardware. Redwood's runtime selects kernels and can run on CPU for small dims but GPUs generally win for batch embedding.
[01:36] Alex Morgan: curious about KV cache — does it help for embeddings?
[01:40] Luis Ortega: typically KV cache is for autoregressive decoders; for embeddings we cache computed vectors for repeated texts, TTL-based. If you have lots of repeated queries, caching hits reduce load significantly. we can cache per-text or per-canonical-id.
[01:56] Dana Lee: our query distribution has a long tail; top 5% queries are 40% traffic, so cache will help.
[02:05] Priya Patel: on indexing: FAISS HNSW is great for low-latency p95s on CPUs for small-ish dims; IVF+PQ reduces memory but adds recall/latency tuning. for your 20M corpus, HNSW on CPU optimized nodes can hit ~10-30ms depending on efSearch and vector dim.
[02:28] Alex Morgan: what's efSearch?
[02:30] Luis Ortega: efSearch is HNSW's search parameter that trades off recall vs latency; higher ef -> better recall, higher latency. common starting ef is 64-128.
[02:38] Samir Patel: running HNSW in memory for 20M at 1024 dims seems big. what's the memory footprint?
[02:44] Priya Patel: rough calc: raw float32 vectors 20M*1024*4 bytes ~ 80 GB raw, plus HNSW graph overhead which can be another 30-60% depending on M parameter. using float16 halves vector bytes; using PQ can shrink to ~8-12 GB but then you pay in lookup/performance.
[03:05] Alex Morgan: so quantization is a big lever. how does Redwood's runtime handle int8 or 4-bit at serving?
[03:11] Luis Ortega: Redwood supports quantized kernels for common model families for embeddings on GPUs — int8 or 4-bit quant inference is supported for certain models, and we have quantized storage for indexes (PQ). for rerankers we caution on quality drift; we recommend A/B evaluation on your dev set.
[03:28] Dana Lee: we care about p99 as well — tail latency spikes kill UI. what operational mitigations exist?
[03:33] Maya Chen: multiple: 1) reserve capacity (Dedicated) to reduce noisy neighbor effects; 2) smart routing + fallback to smaller model variants; 3) request-level timeouts and graceful degrade to cached or cheaper path; 4) KV and prefix caching where applicable.
[03:49] Samir Patel: at 100 QPS, what hardware mix generally?
[03:53] Priya Patel: for 100 QPS first-stage embedding generation if you're generating on the fly on GPU, a few A100-ish GPUs can handle it depending on batch size. Alternatively, precompute embeddings and keep ANN on CPU nodes; then CPU-based ANN can serve 100+ qps with optimized HNSW and enough cores. Reranker (neural) for top-100 can be batched — running on GPU for low latency is helpful.
[04:18] Alex Morgan: batch sizes — what's recommended for E2E latency?
[04:21] Luis Ortega: small batches reduce latency but underutilize GPU. for embedding gen, if you can tolerate 10-20ms extra queuing, batching to 16-32 can be much cheaper. for reranker, batch top_k together — e.g., batch of 100 rerank items per request is natural. Redwood's runtime has dynamic batching with max latency cap you set.
[04:40] Dana Lee: you said dynamic batching — how is the max cap enforced?
[04:42] Priya Patel: we expose a target max_wait_ms; the runtime will hold requests up to that time to form larger batches. you pick a p95 latency SLO and a batch policy. there's also continuous batching heuristics to adapt to traffic.
[04:56] Samir Patel: cost numbers — rough comparison CPU vs GPU for serving ANN and rerank?
[05:00] Maya Chen: rough thumb: CPU ANN storage + queries (HNSW) on 96-256 core instance family tends to be cheaper for large static indexes; GPUs shine for embedding gen and rerank. depending on qps and target latency, Dedicated GPU pool amortized can be cost efficient. we'll share a cost model template.
[05:18] Alex Morgan: re-ranking models — we plan a light cross-encoder (BERT-mini) for top-100 rerank. what's typical lat distribution?
[05:24] Luis Ortega: a BERT-mini on GPU for batch of 100 can be ~30-80ms depending on model size and kernel. on CPU it's usually much higher. quantizing the reranker can help but verify quality.
[05:38] Dana Lee: how does index persistence behave in Private deployment? restarts, warmup?
[05:43] Priya Patel: Private gives you control — we support persistent on-disk indexes with mmap so warmup is minimized; you can pre-warm on boot. for large indexes we recommend keeping them resident in memory on nodes. our console shows cache hit rates and index memory.
[05:58] Alex Morgan: any gotchas with vector dims and PQ with recall?
[06:01] Luis Ortega: PQ is sensitive to dims; higher dims typically compress better per-subvector. splitting dims into too many subquantizers can hurt recall. also, for reranking pipelines we recommend not over-compressing the top-K candidates since reranker will need high-quality candidates.
[06:18] Samir Patel: what about p99 tails from GC or CPU thrashing?
[06:21] Maya Chen: on JVM-based index servers, GC can spike p99s; we generally recommend native processes and pinned memory for ANN; Redwood Dedicated uses tuned node images to minimize OS jitter and has CPU isolation options in Private.
[06:40] Alex Morgan: for our 20M corp at 512 dims, can you give a rough perf estimate?
[06:45] Priya Patel: rough back-of-envelope: 20M x 512 float16 ~ 20M*512*2 bytes ~ 20 GB raw; HNSW overhead maybe +10-30% so ~25 GB. On a 48 core CPU node with optimized FAISS HNSW, p95 ~ 15-40ms depending on efSearch, and throughput hundreds qps per node. For reranker on GPU, batch top100 -> p95 ~ 50-120ms. E2E you'd be in 65-160ms range typically, depending on batching.
[07:10] Dana Lee: sounds promising. we worry about variability when traffic spikes.
[07:14] Luis Ortega: that's where autoscaling plus pinned capacity helps, and also fallback to smaller model or cached responses. Redwood's routing can spill to a cheaper region or fall back to a cached answer if query is recognized.
[07:27] Alex Morgan: do you have benchmark artifacts or config templates?
[07:30] Maya Chen: yes we'll share a benchmark spreadsheet and Redwood config templates for HNSW/IVF+PQ, and a sample cost model.
[07:36] Samir Patel: about quantization — 4-bit seems tempting for embeddings storage, is that production-ready?
[07:42] Luis Ortega: 4-bit storage can drastically reduce index size; inference with 4-bit quant requires careful calibration. For embeddings storage (PQ) it's ok if you accept some recall loss; for on-the-fly embedding generation using quantized models, quality depends on the model and calibration. We recommend running a 5-10% sample eval comparing 4-bit vs float16 on your dev set.
[07:58] Dana Lee: what metrics should we include in the eval?
[08:01] Priya Patel: include recall@k, MRR, p95/p99 latency, memory footprint, cost per qps, and subjective A/B for top-k quality. also log failure modes.
[08:12] Alex Morgan: ok next, VPC details — can Redwood's Private deployment access our KMS?
[08:16] Maya Chen: yes, Private supports customer KMS/HSM integrations and SSO. we'll need network peering or private link; our security docs outline options.
[08:25] Samir Patel: how about audit logs and SOC2 evidence?
[08:28] Priya Patel: Redwood provides audit logs, SAML SSO, RBAC and we have SOC2 + ISO artifacts we can share in the security packet.
[08:36] Alex Morgan: great. any notes on replica placement for HA to keep tail latency low?
[08:41] Luis Ortega: put replicas in separate fault domains and keep read capacity local to region; for strict p99 targets keep standby capacity and use health-based routing to avoid fog.
[08:54] Dana Lee: any examples of batch sizing numbers that are cost-optimal but keep p95 under 30ms?
[08:59] Priya Patel: for embedding lookup probes on GPU, if generation cost dominates, batching to 8-16 is often sweet spot; for pure ANN lookups on CPU, batching is less relevant since queries are independent, focus on concurrency and cores.
[09:14] Samir Patel: can you show us how Redwood's console surfaces the latency breakdown?
[09:18] Maya Chen: we have token-level / request-level breakdowns and per-route dashboards. we'll attach screenshots in the follow-up.
[09:25] Alex Morgan: about SDK integration, do you have examples for streaming top-k and then reranker hooks?
[09:31] Luis Ortega: yes we have SDK snippets for two-stage flows, including streaming embeddings and incremental rerank, we'll share links.
[09:38] Dana Lee: ok let's recap next steps now.
[09:41] Maya Chen: sure. recap: Redwood to run a small benchmark on our side using customer's sample dataset (we'll provide 100k subset), share HNSW and IVF+PQ configs, provide cost model and benchmark spreadsheet, and propose Dedicated vs Private sizing. schedule follow up 2 weeks out.
[09:58] Alex Morgan: timeline works. also want security packet before next call.
[10:02] Priya Patel: we'll attach security docs and SOC2 artifacts.
[10:05] Samir Patel: action items for us: provide 100k sample + queries, and traffic shape.
[10:10] Maya Chen: perfect, we'll follow up with links and an invite. thanks everyone.
[10:15] (call ends)
